record.details: Śūrasena asks Indra what Kṛtavīrya’s father did next. Indra says the son-seeking king anxiously considers childlessness after hearing the Sankaṣṭa and dūrvā accounts. Verse3 calls the dreamer Kārtavīrya, while the waking king is explicitly Kṛtavīrya in13; the name variation is retained. He dreams of his father. They embrace, unable to speak through emotion. The father takes his hand, seats him and says Nārada reported his efforts for a son, prompting the father’s visit to Brahmā. Brahmā prescribed Sankaṣṭa-caturthī and promised offspring to the royal son once the vow removes sin. The father says the book was written according to Brahmā’s instructions, gives it, and tells him to practice for a year so Siddhivināyaka will be pleased and a son will result.
record.outcome: The father delivers a book and prospective remedy in the dream; the printed dreamer name remains under review.

record.details: Himavat tells Pārvatī of the vow practiced by Candraṅgada and his wife Indumatī. The king rules Karṇa city in Mālava, knows Vedas and śāstras, sacrifices and gives generously, and has a brilliant court. Verse 3 prints aṇimādiguṇāpeta: literally free from qualities such as aṇimā. The printed negative qualifier is retained, without emending it to guṇopeta or attributing miraculous perfections. Indumatī is virtuous, serves her husband and parents-in-law, handles household duties and worships gods and guests. Ministers strongly urge the king to abandon the grievously sinful killing involved in hunting.
record.outcome: Royal family and ministers’ warning introduced; printed absence qualifier preserved literally, with no supernatural perfection granted.

record.details: The child announces a means of killing the demon and directs the gods to carry it out. The following strategy clause is preserved as sarvair bhavadbhis taṃ dṛṣṭvā nodanīyo balād aham; its exact intended action remains unresolved. He tells them to watch his and the demon’s remarkable encounter. They joyfully yet uncertainly discuss his capacity and bow. Analāsura approaches as dissolution-fire, burning ten directions and devouring humans. The people cry out and sages flee, warning the child to escape before the fire kills him, comparing it with a great predator. Gaṇeśa stands firm like Himavat; they retreat far away, leaving him there.
